newsitem.title: FRANCE: France says it won't achieve 3.0 pct deficit in 97.
newsitem.headline: France says it won't achieve 3.0 pct deficit in 97.

text.p: France's new left-wing government said for the first time on Thursday it would definitely not reach the Maastricht treaty target of limiting its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year.

But Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn stressed Paris was committed to launching a single European currency on time in 1999 and said the Socialist-led government had no intention of letting deficits run out of control.
Strauss-Kahn's told a business conference France's public deficit in 1997, the crucial measurement year for economic and monetary union (EMU), would be neither three nor 3.1 percent.

"What I can see as clearly as everyone is that we are not at the three percent set in the Finance Act. When you say you are not at three percent, that also means you are not at 3.1 percent either, but I cannot tell you how far we are beyond that," he told the Forum de l'Expansion conference.
"I have no intention, and nor does the prime minister, of allowing any deficit to run out of control," Strauss-Kahn said.
"The government does indeed intend to put France in a position to be able to meet its international commitments concerning the single currency at the planned date," he added.

He gave few details except to say that a cut in Value Added Tax on basic goods, promised by the left during last month's parliamentary election campaign, would have to wait until next year because of the state of public finances.

Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, who campaigned against imposing further austerity to qualify for EMU, has said France's finances are in a serious state and ordered an independent audit to report on July 21.

Jospin's spokesman Manuel Valls told reporters the three percent deficit target was not explicitly mentioned in spending guidelines Jospin sent to ministers for drawing up the 1998 budget and the criterion should be interpreted "as a trend."
Jospin told ministers to give "absolute priority" to fighting unemployment and injustice while respecting France's European Union commitments.

Valls said the instructions were contained in "framework letters" which the prime minister sends each year to ministers setting guidelines for preparing the budget, which did not set any target figure for the 1998 deficit.

Ministers must "include two essential elements, the absolute priority to the fight for employment and for social justice, while respecting our European commitments to achieve economic and monetary union at the deadline foreseen by the treaty".
Strauss-Kahn earlier told the Senate that the government planned to maintain the level of 1997 public deficits left by its conservative predecessors.
New spending measures announced in the government's first policy statement last week would not worsen this year's deficit, he told the upper house of parliament.
Asked how the measures would be financed, he said: "The plan is to maintain the deficit rather than anything else."
Extra spending of between 10 to 15 billion francs ($1.7-2.6 billion) would be balanced by 10 to 15 billion francs of expenditure cut elsewhere, Strauss-Kahn said.
"In any case, there will be in no way an aggravation of the deficit due to these new expenditures," he said.

Valls also said that contrary to a report in the newspaper Le Monde, no decision had been taken yet on whether to go ahead with selling a minority stake in France Telecom, as the previous centre-right government had planned to do.
